name: Grace Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government; what you say stays confidential. Walk me through an ordinary workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Grace Patel, 27, and I run a small finishing crew on building sites. Before anyone starts I mark the tricky joins, check the delivery list on my phone and give the apprentice a clear piece to own. By afternoon I'm fitting trim or repairing what a drawing missed; I love the neat final line and hate sending someone back because a supplier sent the wrong size.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do you stand with the work and the money right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've a trade certificate and I'm among the best carpenters on our sites, so my pay is high for the job. I rent alone and have well over six months of savings, with plenty of other building firms nearby. I use AI on my phone every day to sort measurements and draft material lists, but the timber gets the last word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew this: A clever phone doesn't level a crooked floor. We can use it for the dull lists, then spend the saved hour fixing the join everyone will actually see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I would be a little disappointed; I've been teaching myself these tools because I thought they'd help a small crew compete. Still, my income feels secure if site work carries on, and my rent doesn't depend on a breakthrough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running finishing jobs and put my usual amount into savings. In the first year I'd keep using AI for a first material list, then check every length against the room before ordering; that's already how I caught a short skirting-board count last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a touch of irritation at the noise around AI. I'd still get a good day's work and a wage from the thing I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with that skirting-board count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone counted the straight walls and missed the little alcove by the radiator. I measured it again, added two lengths, and we didn't have to return to the supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy more tools if AI disappoints?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when a paying job needs them. My uncle taught me that a shiny saw on credit is still a bill, and I like keeping my savings free.

say: I would use AI for **dull lists** while my crew fixes visible joins.
I would remind coworkers that a phone cannot **level floors**.
think: My **finishing pay** stays secure if construction carries on.
I feel some **disappointment** because I hoped tools would help small crews compete.
do: Keep **running finishing jobs** for full paid shifts on the current building sites.
Check **AI material lists** against room measurements before ordering.
feel: **Calm**, with mild irritation at exaggerated claims.
S0.quote: A clever phone doesn't level a crooked floor.
fieldNote: Grace already uses AI daily, yet her **measurement habit** stops her treating an automated list as an order.
High pay, **long savings** and local work make the plateau financially comfortable; her disappointment concerns missed opportunity.

steps.text: Keep leading paid finishing jobs on building sites
Check AI material lists against each room before ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site manager to show us the new schedule before promising a client a finish date. Planning software might save the office time, but I want the people fitting the doors to say where the bottleneck is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my ability to check layouts against real rooms could become more valuable while office planners shrink. Yet contractors might use the software savings to press our day rate, and I could lose hours between jobs if every crew bids faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd offer to test the new scheduling tool on one occupied-house renovation, with the owner agreeing to the trial. During the first year I'd compare its delivery slots with actual fitting hours, show the manager the misses, and keep taking normal paid site shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can probably keep earning, but I don't want a quick computer estimate used as proof that my crew is slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it gives us one day to hang ten doors where the old frames all need packing, that's a miss. I'd photograph the frame gaps and note our hours, not just complain over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try another contractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are plenty close by, but I'd ask them about rates only if ours were cut. I don't want to move a crew for a rumour.

say: I would ask to see the **schedule** before a finish date is promised.
I would insist that fitters explain real **bottlenecks** to managers.
think: My **layout checks** may gain value as office planning shrinks.
My **hours** could dip if fast bids put pressure on crew rates.
do: Test the **scheduling tool** on one agreed renovation.
Record **frame gaps** and fitting hours to challenge bad estimates.
Keep taking **paid shifts** while comparing results.
feel: **Uneasy** about computer estimates being used to judge crew speed.
S1.quote: I don't want a quick computer estimate used as proof that my crew is slow.
fieldNote: She sees a possible new role checking plans on site, but her own **hours** could realistically fall under faster bidding.
Her response is to gather **measured evidence** from a specific renovation while continuing the work that pays her rent.

steps.text: Test scheduling tool on one renovation with owner agreement
Keep taking paid finishing shifts while recording frame gaps and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI can take the drawing and ordering work in 2028, but don't mistake a clean drawing for a clean room. We have until about 2031 before robots can fit and repair like we do, if this card is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role includes planning, so some of my best-paid time could disappear in 2028, before the physical work goes. By 2031 I expect contractors to need fewer finishers . My savings buy time to switch, but they won't pay my rent for decades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this winter I'd book a short course in surveying old buildings and keep my finishing shifts. In 2029 I'd ask two local renovation firms for paid trial days checking hidden damage on site, while AI handles drawings; before 2031 I'd decide whether that work has enough customers to make a business worth funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even with money put aside. I can move, but a three-year bridge is short when the hands-on trade that pays me is next in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would surveying old buildings survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It may not; robots could eventually lift boards and inspect the damage too. I'm betting there will be a period when owners still want a trusted person in an old house, and I'll test that with paid days rather than a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my apprentice to keep learning the craft and keep receipts for every small repair job. I couldn't honestly promise that the full crew will be on the same site in 2031.

say: I would explain that **2028 AGI** reaches drawings before hands-on robots reach sites.
I would warn apprentices that **2031 robots** could cut finishing crews.
think: My **planning pay** could shrink in 2028 before physical work does.
My **finishing income** could fall sharply when robots arrive around 2031.
do: Book a **building survey** course while keeping site shifts.
Ask two firms for **paid trial days** inspecting old houses in 2029.
Test demand before using savings for a **business**.
feel: **Anxious** about a short bridge before robot competition.
S2.quote: My savings buy time to switch, but they won't pay my rent for decades.
fieldNote: Her team lead duties make **2028 AGI** an income risk even before robots can handle fitting work.
She treats old-house surveying as a **paid experiment**, explicitly admitting robots could later challenge that work.

steps.text: Book a short course in surveying old buildings this winter
Ask two renovation firms for paid trial inspection days in 2029
Keep working paid finishing shifts during the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five years are useful only if we try real alternatives before everyone else arrives at the same door. The thinking side turns in 2031 and the fitting robots arrive around 2034; those are two different deadlines for my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32, I could lose some lead hours when AGI handles plans and ordering, although site repairs should still bring work. At 35, robots that can fit as well as people could cut my paid days badly. Being one of the better carpenters doesn't create more customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start taking one small paid restoration job each quarter and write down the true hours, without leaving the main contractor. By 2032 I'd use AGI to quote those jobs and compare it with my own figures; in the first year after AGI arrives I'd seek a formal role managing several repair sites, before the 2034 robot change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though less rushed than in the two-year version. Five years gives me room to see whether household repairs actually pay, instead of selling myself a business idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first restoration job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A landlord has asked me to repair the sash window in a vacant flat; I'd price the wood and one day's labour before saying yes. If the frame is rotten deeper in, I'll show the landlord the extra work before cutting it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire the apprentice for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I can pay a proper day rate out of the price, yes. I won't call unpaid help a training opportunity just to make the sums look good.

say: I would stress that **2031 planning** and **2034 robots** are separate deadlines.
I would push the crew to try **paid alternatives** while current jobs remain.
think: My **lead hours** may shrink once AGI handles plans.
My **paid site days** could fall badly when fitting robots arrive.
do: Take one **paid restoration job** each quarter and record hours.
Use **AGI quotes** against my own numbers by 2032.
Seek a **multi-site repair** role after AGI arrives.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to test demand before committing savings.
S3.quote: Being one of the better carpenters doesn't create more customers.
fieldNote: Grace keeps her **main contractor** while testing restoration demand, a distinct path from starting a business on faith.
She distinguishes a **2031 planning** shock from the later 2034 physical work shock and expects wage pressure at both points.

steps.text: Take one paid restoration job each quarter while employed
Compare AGI restoration quotes with own figures by 2032
Seek a paid multi-site repair management role after 2031
Keep paid shifts with the main contractor while testing demand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger crew that ten years is a chance to get very good at something and teach it, not a promise of permanent jobs. I'll be 37 at AGI in 2036 and 40 when the fitting robots come around 2039, with a lot of working life still ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can earn well through much of the decade and build a small restoration service if real customers keep paying. Once robots can do site work, neither my trade certificate nor my speed guarantees a wage; the longer runway makes the loss manageable, not imaginary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd put a fixed part of each high-paying contract into savings and take one restoration commission a quarter. Over the decade I'd train an apprentice for paid old-house work; in 2037 I'd use AGI to handle bookings and quotes, then compare the service's profit with my site wage before buying a workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened today. The time lets me build proof in a ledger, but I don't want to be 40 with a shed of tools and no paying clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a house in that period?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I rent now and may buy if the numbers work, but I wouldn't tie all my savings up just to say I own a place. My mother always said a roof is valuable only if you can keep paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the restoration idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the quarterly jobs don't cover the apprentice's wage, materials and my time, I'd stop expanding it. I could still use those skills as an employee while I look for other work.

say: I would tell apprentices that **ten years** offers time to build skills.
I would say **2039 robots** still threaten site wages at age 40.
think: My **site income** may remain strong for much of the decade.
My **certificate** cannot guarantee paid work after capable robots arrive.
do: Add a fixed share of contracts to **savings**.
Take quarterly **restoration commissions** and pay an apprentice for real work.
Use **AGI bookings** in 2037 before deciding on a workshop.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2039 wages, with time to test a service.
S4.quote: I don't want to be 40 with a shed of tools and no paying clients.
fieldNote: Her ten-year path rests on **paid customers** and recorded profit, not an assumption that hand skill stays scarce forever.
She retains **site wages** while saving, teaching an apprentice and testing whether a workshop would have enough demand.

steps.text: Put a fixed share of each high-paying contract into savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 version worries me most because my planning hours get hit first and robots can reach the fitting work by 2031. I'd want an affordable course with access to real old-building jobs, and contractors willing to pay trial days rather than asking for free work. A bridge from my current site wage matters more than a glossy forecast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays the apprentice during all this testing. I can afford to try a course, but a new worker may have only this week's wage. If I take them onto a restoration job, I need to put their proper pay in the quote from the start.

headlineQuote: A bridge from my current site wage matters more than a glossy forecast.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** finishing crew lead with high pay, strong savings and many nearby builders.
She uses **AI daily**, checking its lists against measurements and inviting site trials.
She expects **planning hours** to shrink before robots threaten hands-on finishing work.
She tests **paid restoration** jobs while keeping site wages and protecting an apprentice’s pay.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** threatens her planning hours quickly and her finishing wage when robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: An **affordable course** and paid trial work in old buildings would bridge her current wage to another role.
